questions.explain: Vector addition in R^n is coordinate-by-coordinate: 2 + 4 = 6 and 3 + (-1) = 2, giving [6, 2].
Scalar multiplication scales every coordinate: 3*2 = 6 and 3*3 = 9, giving [6, 9].

questions.q: A single qubit's state is best described as:
options: A vector in C^2, the space of ordered pairs of complex numbers
A single real number between 0 and 1
A vector in R^2 only, since qubit coordinates are always real
questions.explain: A qubit's state lives in C^2: a 2-entry vector whose entries can be complex, with |0> = [1,0] and |1> = [0,1] as the two computational basis states.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the vector space axioms?
options: Every vector must have a length of exactly 1
Addition is commutative: u + v = v + u
There exists a zero vector 0 such that v + 0 = v
Scalar multiplication distributes over vector addition: a(u + v) = au + av
questions.explain: Nothing in the vector space axioms requires vectors to have length 1 -- that's a separate normalization condition (relevant to valid quantum states, covered in Lesson 3), not part of the definition of a vector space itself.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a vector like [2, 3] is really 'relative to a chosen basis' rather than an absolute identity?
options: Because the same underlying vector can be written with different coordinate numbers if you change which basis directions you measure against
Because [2, 3] is not technically a valid vector in any space
Because vectors in R^2 cannot be added to vectors in C^2
Because only qubit states, not ordinary R^2 vectors, depend on a basis
questions.explain: Coordinates like [2, 3] describe a vector as a combination of specific basis directions; changing the basis (covered in Lesson 4) changes the numbers even though the vector itself is unchanged.
